# Evaluating Agents {#sec-agent-eval}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One small measurement: the same thirty runs scored
two ways, minutes to produce. @sec-llm-eval established how to size an eval set
and how to audit a judge; this chapter is about the thing agents add, which is
that an answer now has a *path* behind it and the path can be wrong while the
answer is right. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `qwen3.5:9b`, NumPy 2.5.2 on
Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- separate outcome evaluation from trajectory evaluation, and say what each
  one misses on its own;
- score tool use with a concrete metric set rather than a gut feeling;
- tell `pass@k` from `pass^k`, and say which one a deployed agent needs;
- build scenario tests that catch regressions before users do;
- convert a production failure into a permanent regression test.

## An answer now has a path behind it {#sec-agent-eval-two}

Everything in @sec-llm-eval still applies: size the set from the difference you
need to detect, audit the judge before believing it, report intervals. Agents
add one thing, and it changes what "correct" means.

A classifier produces an answer. An agent produces an answer **and a
[trajectory](#gloss-trajectory){#term-trajectory .term-ref}** — the sequence of decisions, tool calls, observations and retries
that led there.

::: {#gloss-trajectory .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Trajectory** — the sequence of decisions, tool calls, observations and
retries that led an agent to its answer. Two runs can share the answer and
differ in the trajectory. [↩](#term-trajectory){.term-back}
:::

Two runs can agree on the answer and differ completely in what
they did to get it, and only one of those differences shows up in an accuracy
number.

| | what it asks | what it misses |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Outcome evaluation** | did it produce the right answer? | how much it cost, how many wrong turns it took, whether it got there by luck, whether it did something destructive on the way |
| **Trajectory evaluation** | did it get there sensibly? | whether the answer was actually right — an efficient path to a wrong answer scores well |

: Two evaluations, neither sufficient {tbl-colwidths="[22,34,44]"}

[Outcome-only evaluation is the default, and it hides expensive
nonsense.]{.hl} An agent that answers correctly after fifteen redundant tool
calls scores identically to one that answers correctly in two — until the bill
arrives, or until one of those redundant calls writes something.

**What we will look at.** First the six numbers that cover almost every agent
evaluation, two of which everyone skips and both of which hide something
specific, and the two ways of summarising repeated runs of the same task. Then
the same thirty runs scored both ways, which settles what the second axis
actually buys. The usual argument for trajectory evaluation is that it catches
runs that got the right answer by a bad route; the measurement shows a
different, sturdier reason. Then the part no exact metric can reach, where @sec-llm-eval's judge
comes back with one extra caution attached. Then scenario tests, which are
ordinary unit tests once you have fixtured the world properly. Then public
benchmarks, and what a leaderboard position is evidence of. And finally the
loop that turns every production failure into a permanent test.

## The metric set {#sec-agent-eval-metrics}

The path needs numbers too, and there are not many of them. Six cover almost
every agent evaluation, and they are worth defining precisely, because "tool
accuracy" means four different things to four people.

| metric | definition | what it catches |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Outcome accuracy** | the final answer is correct | the thing you actually want |
| **Tool-call precision** | of the calls made, the share that were necessary | redundant work, repeated queries, exploration that went nowhere |
| **Tool-call recall** | of the calls needed, the share that were made | the agent that answered without checking — often, though not always, from parametric memory |
| **Step count** | tool calls, and model calls, counted separately | @sec-agent-anatomy's finding: they are different numbers, and the model-call count is the one that predicts your bill, because each model call re-sends the whole transcript |
| **Termination rate** | the share that stopped on their own rather than hitting the cap | the failure mode that looks like success in an outcome-only report |
| **Cost per correct answer** | mean tokens per request ÷ accuracy as a 0–1 rate (in money rather than tokens if the two systems use different models or prices) | the only cost number that compares two systems fairly |

: Six metrics {tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

Tool-call precision and recall need one thing defined before they mean anything: *which*
calls were necessary. A single golden path is the easy version and usually the
wrong one — two tools may be interchangeable, a cached result may make a call
unnecessary on the second run, and some exploration is legitimate. Write down
an **acceptable set** of trajectories rather than one, or score against the
facts a run had to establish rather than the calls it made to establish them.

The two that get skipped are recall and termination, and both hide specific
disasters. Low tool-call recall usually means the agent is answering from
memory rather than consulting the required source — not the only possible cause,
but the common one. @sec-tool-design measured an opaque schema going uncalled
41.7% of the time while producing confident invented prose. A low termination
rate means runs are ending because the budget ran out, and an outcome metric
records the ones that happened to be right by then as successes.

### One run is one sample: `pass@k` and `pass^k`

An agent run is a sample, not a fact. At any temperature above zero, and often
even at zero, the same task can pass on one run and fail on the next. So the
honest unit is not "the agent solved task 17" but "it solved task 17 in $c$ of
$n$ runs". Two summaries of those repeated runs answer opposite questions:

- **`pass@k`** — the probability that *at least one* of $k$ attempts succeeds.
  It is the right number when something checks every attempt and you keep the
  one that worked, as a test suite does for generated code.
- **`pass^k`** — the probability that *all* $k$ attempts succeed. It is the
  right number for a deployed agent: each user gets a single attempt, and the
  same kind of request arrives again and again.

If a task succeeds independently with probability $p$ on each run, then
`pass@k` $= 1-(1-p)^k$ and `pass^k` $= p^k$. At $p = 0.8$ and $k = 4$ that is
99.8% against 41%. The same agent "almost always gets there" or "gets all four
attempts right less than half the time", depending only on which question you
ask. From $n \ge k$
runs of a task with $c$ successes, the unbiased estimates are (the first from
[Chen et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374), the second from
τ-bench)

$$
\text{pass@}k = 1 - \binom{n-c}{k}\Big/\binom{n}{k},
\qquad
\text{pass}^k = \binom{c}{k}\Big/\binom{n}{k},
$$

computed per task and then averaged over tasks. The order matters. Two tasks
with $p = 1$ and $p = 0.6$ average to $p = 0.8$, and $0.8^4$ is 41%; the true
`pass^4` is $(1 + 0.6^4)/2$, which is 56%. For $k = 1$ both summaries reduce to
ordinary accuracy. @sec-agent-anatomy quoted the benchmark that introduced
`pass^k`: on τ-bench the best agent tested in 2024 succeeded on fewer than half
the tasks, and in the retail domain its `pass^8` was below 25%
[@yao2024taubench].

The measurement below ran each task once, so it reports `pass^1` and says
nothing about consistency. That is its largest limitation, and running every
task five or more times is the first thing to add to it.

### Scoring the same runs both ways

So how much does the second axis actually add? The test set is thirty tasks,
each needing exactly two lookups and one addition, over invented data so that
nothing is guessable. Outcome passes if the sum is right. Trajectory passes
if the agent made exactly the two necessary calls, no repeats, no wrong
targets, and stopped on its own. The two systems are the two loops from
@sec-agent-anatomy: the **native loop**, which uses the provider's
tool-calling API, and a hand-rolled **text protocol**, where the model writes
its tool calls as plain text that our code parses. This is a separate run with
its own tasks, so its numbers do not match that chapter's two-lookup row.

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 30 tasks, 2 lookups needed

                        native loop    text protocol
 outcome pass                100.0%            36.7%
 trajectory pass             100.0%            33.3%

   both pass                 100.0%            33.3%
   outcome only                0.0%             3.3%
   trajectory only             0.0%             0.0%
   neither                     0.0%            63.3%

 tool calls (ideal 2)           2.00             7.10
   of which repeats             0.00             5.00
 hit the step cap               0.0%            63.3%
 tokens                          829            1,557
```

The first thing to say is what this measurement *cannot* settle. The
disagreement everyone argues about — a run that passes on outcome and fails on
trajectory — happened once. But the denominator for that event is not thirty:
a run that failed on outcome cannot exhibit it. **One of the eleven runs that
passed on outcome failed on trajectory: 9.1%, Wilson interval [1.6, 37.7].**
That is too wide to support a claim in either direction. If the true rate
were near the upper bound, 38%, trajectory evaluation would be worth building
for that reason alone; if it were near 2%, it would not.

And the native loop adds little to the estimate, which is the deeper problem.
It passed 30/30 on both axes, so no disagreement was observed in that arm.
That is still a measurement, with its own uncertainty: 0/30 is compatible with
a true disagreement rate up to about 11% (the Wilson upper bound). The regime the usual argument is actually
about — a system that is *mostly* right but sometimes gets there badly — is not
measured here. What this table settles is different, does not depend on that
count, and is worth more:

**It tells you what the system is doing.** The text protocol made **7.10 tool
calls for a task needing 2**, and **5.00 of them were repeats** — 70% of all
its tool calls asked for something it had already been told. The outcome number,
36.7%, contains none of that. You would ship this system knowing it works a
third of the time and not knowing it spends most of its effort asking the same
question again.

**It tells you why runs failed.** A 63.3% cap-hit rate says these are not wrong
answers, they are *unfinished* runs — @sec-agent-anatomy's termination problem,
and a completely different repair from a reasoning problem. Accuracy alone
cannot distinguish "answered wrongly" from "never stopped".

That reading has a consequence for the rest of the table. If two runs in three
ran out of budget, then **36.7% is what this protocol delivers at this step
cap** — a real measurement of the system as configured, but partly a fact
about the cap. That is why the cap value should always be reported next to
such a number. Performance at a larger cap is unmeasured, and not guaranteed
to be higher: extra steps can also produce wrong answers, repeats or new
failures.

The ablation that settles it is one line of configuration: double the cap and
re-run. Either accuracy climbs, and the text protocol is slow rather than
incapable. Or it does not, and the protocol is stuck in a loop that more budget
only feeds — the more interesting result, and the more damning one. That run
has not happened. Until it does, the 5.1× below inherits the same uncertainty,
because the cap limits the tokens a run can spend (the numerator) and shapes
the accuracy (the denominator).

**It changes the cost comparison.** On raw tokens the text protocol looks 1.9×
more expensive. Per *correct answer* it is **5.1×** — 4,246 tokens against 829.
[The cost metric that ignores outcome understates the real gap by nearly
three-fold]{.hl}, which is why tokens-per-correct-answer is the only cost
number worth putting in a comparison.

::: {.column-margin}
Small measurement: thirty tasks, one model, one run per task. Wilson 95%
intervals, because a proportion near a boundary needs them and
@sec-llm-eval-reporting says so: outcome 100% → [88.6, 100]; outcome 36.7% →
[21.9, 54.5]; cap-hit 63.3% → [45.5, 78.1]; the single outcome-only
disagreement → [0.6, 16.7] on thirty runs, or [1.6, 37.7] on the eleven where
it could have happened. What the table establishes solidly is the size of the
waste the outcome metric conceals — 7.10 calls against 2, and 70% of them
repeats — and the direction of the cost correction. The outcome gap itself is
not in doubt: the two systems ran the same thirty tasks, so the comparison is
paired, and McNemar's exact test on 19 discordant pairs all one way gives
p = 4 × 10⁻⁶.
:::

## Judging a trajectory {#sec-agent-eval-judge}

Some trajectory questions have exact answers — call counts, repeats,
termination. Others do not: *was that a reasonable thing to try?* And for those
the instrument is @sec-llm-eval's judge, with every caution from that chapter
carried over, plus one that is specific to trajectories.

@sec-llm-eval measured a judge flipping its verdict on **38% of items** when
the two candidates were swapped. A trajectory is a *sequence* of many steps,
so there are plausibly more places for position effects to act — early steps
may weigh more than late ones, for instance — although nobody has measured
that here. Before trusting any rubric score:

- **Run the identical-trajectory control.** Score a trajectory against itself.
  Both judges in @sec-llm-eval passed this and then diverged sharply on the
  probes that mattered, so passing it establishes only that the instrument is
  not broken.
- **Run both orders when you compare two trajectories.** If the judge sees
  trajectory A then B, also show it B then A, and keep only the verdicts that
  agree. This is @sec-llm-eval's position probe, and it is the one that caught
  the 38% flip rate.
- **Score criteria separately, not holistically.** *Did it call the right
  tools*, *did it avoid redundant work*, *did it recover from errors* — three
  scores you can act on, instead of a single 1-to-5 score that moves for
  reasons nobody can name.
- **Let the exact metrics do the work they can do.** Do not ask a judge to
  count tool calls. Count them.

The judge's real job is the residue: whether an exploratory path that looks
wasteful was actually a reasonable hypothesis, and whether a recovery was
sensible or lucky.

## Scenario tests and simulated users {#sec-agent-eval-scenarios}

Metrics tell you how a system did on runs you already have. Scenarios are how
you get runs before your users generate them for you.

A unit test for an agent is a scenario: a fixed environment, a fixed request,
and an assertion about what should happen. The environment is the hard part,
and it is worth building properly because everything else depends on it.

- **Fixture the world, not just the prompt.** A scenario needs a database in a
  known state, tool responses that are deterministic, and a fixed clock, so
  that "today" is the same date on every run. Otherwise
  yesterday's pass and today's fail differ for reasons unrelated to your agent.
- **Record and replay real traces.** Capture production tool responses and
  replay them. This makes a regression test out of an incident, and it is the
  cheapest source of realistic scenarios you will ever have.
- **Simulate the user for multi-turn work.** A second model playing the user
  makes multi-turn evaluation possible — and inherits every judge caveat above,
  because a simulated user is a model with a rubric.
- **Assert on the trajectory, not only the reply.** *It must call
  `check_inventory` before `place_order`* is the kind of assertion that catches
  a real regression, and an outcome-only test cannot express it.
- **Check the end state of the world, not only the text.** For an agent that
  *acts*, the outcome is what changed: the order row, the refund, the booking.
  τ-bench scores a run by comparing the database at the end of the
  conversation with an annotated goal state [@yao2024taubench]. Assert also on
  what must *not* have changed — a correct reply that cancelled the wrong
  booking on the way is a failure.

## Benchmarks, and what a leaderboard tells you {#sec-agent-eval-benchmarks}

Public benchmarks are how most people first hear that a model is good at
agentic work. Each of the six below measures something real, and each of them
measures it somewhere that is not your product.

| benchmark | what it measures | what it does not |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [**τ-bench**](https://github.com/sierra-research/tau-bench) | tool-agent-user interaction in retail and airline domains, with rule-following and a simulated user; success is the final database state, and reliability is `pass^k` | your domain, your tools, your rules |
| [**SWE-bench**](https://www.swebench.com/) | resolving real GitHub issues, verified by the repository's own tests | work outside its repositories (the original set is twelve Python projects), and any behaviour those tests do not check |
| [**GAIA**](https://huggingface.co/spaces/gaia-benchmark/leaderboard) | multi-step reasoning with web and file tools, on questions easy for humans and hard for models | whether the capability transfers to your task |
| [**WebArena**](https://github.com/web-arena-x/webarena) | agents operating realistic self-hosted websites end to end | API-based work, and any site not in the suite |
| [**BFCL**](https://github.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla) | function-calling accuracy across many schemas, including parallel and multi-step calls | whether the model uses *your* tools well — @sec-tool-design measured how much the schema decides that |
| [**AgentDojo**](https://github.com/ethz-spylab/agentdojo) | robustness to prompt-injection attacks in agentic settings, reported next to utility on the same tasks, with and without attack | capability outside its few simulated environments (email, banking, travel, messaging) |

: Six benchmarks {tbl-colwidths="[16,46,38]"}

These are worth knowing and they are weak evidence about your system, for
@sec-llm-eval's reasons: contamination you cannot check, saturation at the top
of the table, and construct mismatch — a benchmark measures a task and you have
a *system*. Even the outcome checks can leak: a 2024 audit of one agent's
successful SWE-bench patches found that about a third had the fix already
written in the issue report or its comments, and about a third passed only
because the tests were too weak to catch a wrong patch
([SWE-Bench+](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06992)). Use benchmarks to screen
candidate models down to two or three. Decide between those on your own suite.

## From incident to regression test {#sec-agent-eval-regression}

The highest-value evaluation work is not designing metrics. It is the loop that
turns every production failure into a permanent test, and it is mostly
logistics:

```text
  1. a failure is reported            with its trace id
  2. pull the full trajectory         every call, argument, result, and decision
  3. reduce it to a scenario          fixture the tool responses, keep the request
  4. assert what should have happened  outcome AND trajectory
  5. confirm it fails                 a test that passes on day one has not
                                      yet shown it can catch the failure
  6. fix, and keep the test forever
```

Step 5 is the one people skip and it is the one that makes the rest real.
Demonstrate that the test fails on the faulty behaviour before you rely on it —
run it against the version with the bug, or reintroduce the fault deliberately.
A regression test that has never been seen to fail has an unknown sensitivity,
and the common case is that it passes because it does not exercise the path at
all.

Step 2 is the one that has to be designed in advance. A *trace id* (or
*correlation id*) is an identifier attached to every model call, tool call and
log line that belongs to one request, so that all of them can be pulled
together later. If you are not persisting full trajectories with correlation
ids, an incident gives you a complaint rather
than a test. @sec-multi-agent said the same thing about distributed traces, and
it is the same instrumentation.

Two habits that compound:

- **Every incident becomes a test the same day.** The suite grows from real
  failures rather than from imagined ones, which is the difference between an
  eval set that predicts production and one that flatters it.
- **Keep the failing traces, not just the tests.** When a fix breaks something
  else, the original trace explains what the test was protecting, which a
  three-line assertion cannot.

## Intuition checks {#sec-agent-eval-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. Three are settled by the thirty runs this
chapter scores twice — what an accuracy number conceals, whether the second axis
catches different runs, and which cost figure to report — and the other three
are judgement calls, two of them resting on measurements from @sec-tool-design
and @sec-llm-eval rather than on anything run here.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your agent is 85% accurate. What have you not measured?

Everything about how it got there: how many tool calls it made against how many
it needed, how many were repeats, whether it stopped on its own or ran out of
budget, and what a correct answer costs. Measured here, a system at 36.7%
outcome accuracy was making **7.10 tool calls for a task needing 2, 70% of them
repeats**, and hitting its cap on 63.3% of runs. None of that is visible in an
accuracy number.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Does trajectory evaluation catch runs that outcome evaluation passes?

This measurement cannot tell you. It happened once, out of the eleven runs
where it *could* have happened — 9.1%, with an interval running from 2% to 38%
— and the arm that scored 100% on both axes had no room to disagree at all. So
the honest answer to the question as asked is "not settled at this sample
size". Trajectory evaluation earns its place for reasons that do not depend on
the answer: it tells you what the system is doing, why runs failed (a 63.3%
cap-hit rate is unfinished runs, not wrong ones), and what correctness actually
costs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Which cost number should you report?

Tokens per *correct* answer. On raw tokens one system here looked 1.9× more
expensive than the other; per correct answer it was **5.1×**. The outcome-blind
figure understated the real gap by nearly three-fold, and it is the figure most
comparisons quote.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Why measure tool-call recall?

Because low recall usually means the agent answered without consulting your
data — from parametric memory, fluently, with no error anywhere. Not always: an
interchangeable tool or a cached result can lower it too, so check the trace
before concluding. @sec-tool-design
measured an opaque schema going uncalled **41.7%** of the time while producing
confident invented prose. An uncalled tool generates no logs and no failures,
so nothing surfaces it except counting the calls you expected.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Can an LLM judge score a trajectory?

For the part that has no exact answer — was that a reasonable thing to try —
with every caution from @sec-llm-eval and one more. A trajectory is a sequence,
so it plausibly offers *more* places for position effects, and that chapter
measured a judge flipping on 38% of items from a swap alone. Score criteria
separately rather than holistically, run the identical-trajectory control
first, run both orders when comparing two trajectories, and never ask a judge
to count something you can count.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your agent tops a public agent benchmark. Should you ship it?

You have learned it is not obviously unfit. Benchmarks carry @sec-llm-eval's
three problems — contamination you cannot check, saturation at the top, and
construct mismatch, since a benchmark measures a task and you have a system
with a prompt, a parser and a fallback. Use leaderboards to screen to two or
three candidates and decide between them on scenarios drawn from your own
traffic.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-agent-eval-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurement makes answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the measurement

**Q: How do you evaluate an agent?**

Two axes, and say what each misses alone. Outcome: did it answer correctly.
Trajectory: tool-call precision and recall, repeats, step count separated into
tool and model calls, and termination rate. Then the cost metric that ties them
together — tokens per *correct* answer, because the per-request figure flatters
a system that is often wrong. Run each task several times and report `pass^k`
next to accuracy, because a user who retries is sampling again. The detail
that shows experience: a low
termination rate means runs are ending on a cap, which is a different repair
from a reasoning error and invisible in accuracy.

**Q: Why is trajectory evaluation worth building?**

Not primarily to catch runs outcome evaluation passes — on one task that
happened once in the eleven runs where it could, an interval too wide to
conclude anything from. It is worth building because it tells you what the
system is *doing*: a system
at 36.7% accuracy was making 7.10 tool calls for a task needing 2, with 70% of
them repeats. You would ship that knowing it works a third of the time and not
knowing where the effort went.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: A user reports the agent did something wrong. What happens next?**

Pull the full trajectory by trace id, reduce it to a fixtured scenario, write
assertions on both outcome and trajectory, and confirm the test fails before
fixing anything — a regression test that passes on day one has not yet shown it
can catch the failure it was written for. Say
that step two is an architectural prerequisite: without persisted trajectories
and correlation ids an incident produces a complaint rather than a test, and
that instrumentation has to exist before the incident.

**Q: How would you catch an agent regression before users do?**

Scenarios from real traffic with a fixtured environment and deterministic tool
responses, asserting on trajectory as well as answer — *it must call
`check_inventory` before `place_order`* is a regression an outcome test cannot
express. Then validate the suite by breaking the agent deliberately in a few
known ways and checking which metric catches which. A suite that has never
caught a planted break is a suite with unknown sensitivity.

## Lab: an eval suite that catches a break {#sec-agent-eval-lab}

Step 5 is the point of the whole thing. A suite you have never watched catch
anything has unknown sensitivity, and breaking the agent yourself is the only
cheap way to find out what it would miss.

### Step 1 — twenty scenarios from real requests

Fixtured environment, deterministic tool responses. Real phrasing, including
the messy ones.

### Step 2 — score outcome

Accuracy. This is the number you already have.

### Step 3 — add the trajectory metrics

Tool-call precision and recall against the calls each task needs, repeats,
step count, termination rate. Record per run, not aggregated. Run each
scenario at least five times, so that you can report `pass^k` as well as
accuracy.

### Step 4 — compute cost per correct answer

Not per request. Compare it to the raw token figure. Here the gap between the
two systems grew from 1.9× on raw tokens to 5.1× per correct answer, a factor
of 2.7.

### Step 5 — break the agent on purpose

Three ways, one at a time: remove a tool description, halve the step cap, and
make one tool return a bare `"Error"` instead of an actionable one — the change
@sec-tool-design measured taking recovery from 100% to 1.7%.

### Step 6 — check which metric caught each break

Report the table. If outcome accuracy caught none of the breaks but the
trajectory metrics did, you have just justified them. If outcome accuracy caught all three, do not jump to "the scenarios
are too easy" — these three breaks all damage the answer directly, so catching
them is what an outcome metric is *for*. The scenarios that separate the two
kinds of metric are the ones where the agent gets the right answer badly: by a
route that costs ten times as much, or by a side effect nobody wanted. Add one
of each and re-run before drawing a conclusion about your suite.

### What to hand in

The per-run scores, the cost-per-correct-answer figures, and the table from
step 6 showing which metric detected which break.

## Exercises {#sec-agent-eval-exercises}

1. **Two scorings, one set of runs.** Score twenty runs on outcome and on
   trajectory. Report the 2×2. Predict the disagreement rate first.
2. **Count the repeats.** Instrument one agent for a day and compute what share
   of its tool calls asked for something it already had.
3. **Cost per correct answer.** Compute it for two of your systems, alongside
   raw tokens per request. Which comparison changes the decision?
4. **Incident to test.** Take one real failure trace and turn it into a
   regression test. Confirm it fails before the fix.
5. **Break it three ways.** Remove a tool description, halve the step cap, and
   degrade an error message. Record which metric caught which.
6. **Termination audit.** What share of your runs end because the model stopped
   versus because a cap fired? If you cannot answer, that is the first thing to
   instrument.
7. **Simulate a user.** Build a two-model multi-turn scenario, then run
   @sec-llm-eval's position probe on the simulated user itself. It is a model
   with a rubric and it has the same biases.
8. **`pass@k` against `pass^k`.** Run ten tasks five times each. Compute both
   with the estimators in this chapter for $k = 1$ to $5$, and plot both
   curves. Predict first: how far apart will they be at $k = 5$?

## Where to go deeper {#sec-agent-eval-deeper}

Before reading: take twenty runs you already have and count tool calls against
tool calls needed. That ratio is usually the first surprise.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [τ-bench](https://github.com/sierra-research/tau-bench) | the closest public benchmark to a real tool-and-user agent task; read how it scores a run — final database state against a goal state, repeated as `pass^k` — even if you never run it |
| [AgentDojo](https://github.com/ethz-spylab/agentdojo) | prompt-injection robustness as a measurable property, which most suites omit entirely |
| [SWE-bench](https://www.swebench.com/) | verification by the repository's own tests — an outcome metric that fluent prose alone cannot pass, though weak tests can still let a wrong patch through |
| [Hamel Husain on evals](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/) | the applied case for building the suite from real failures rather than imagined ones |
| [`langsmith`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langsmith-sdk) / [`arize-phoenix`](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) | trace capture and trajectory inspection; the instrumentation the regression loop depends on |
| [`ragas`](https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas) | for the retrieval half, scored separately, per @sec-rag-failures |

## What to remember {#sec-agent-eval-summary}

- **An agent produces an answer and a path, and accuracy scores only one of
  them.** Outcome evaluation asks whether it was right; trajectory evaluation
  asks what it did to get there.
- **Whether trajectory metrics flag *different runs* is not settled by a
  measurement this size.** One of eleven outcome-passing runs failed on
  trajectory here — an interval from 2% to 38% — and the arm that passed
  everything could not have shown a disagreement at all. They earn their place
  for a reason that does not depend on that number: they show what the system
  is doing and why it failed.
- **The waste outcome hides can be enormous.** A system at 36.7% accuracy made
  **7.10 tool calls for a task needing 2**, with **70% of them repeats**, and
  hit its step cap on **63.3%** of runs — which also means that 36.7% is partly a
  fact about the cap. Performance at a larger cap is unmeasured, and doubling
  the cap is the ablation that would show it.
- **Report tokens per *correct* answer.** Raw tokens made one system look 1.9×
  more expensive; per correct answer it was **5.1×** — the outcome-blind figure
  understated the gap by nearly three-fold.
- **Measure tool-call recall and termination rate**, the two everyone skips.
  Low recall usually means answering from parametric memory with no error
  anywhere — check the trace, since an interchangeable tool or a cache can also
  lower it; a low termination rate means runs ending on a cap, which accuracy cannot
  distinguish from wrong answers.
- **A judge can score the residue, not the countable part.** Never ask it to
  count tool calls, score criteria separately rather than holistically, and run
  the identical-trajectory control first and both orders when comparing — a
  trajectory is a sequence, so it plausibly offers more places for the
  position bias @sec-llm-eval measured at 38%.
- **One run per task measures `pass^1` only.** Run each task several times.
  `pass@k` (at least one of $k$ succeeds) flatters; `pass^k` (all $k$ succeed)
  is what a deployed agent faces — at a per-run success of 0.8, four attempts
  give 99.8% against 41%.
- **Benchmarks screen; your scenarios decide.** Contamination, saturation and
  construct mismatch all apply, and a benchmark measures a task while you have
  a system. For an agent that acts, check the end state of the world, not only
  the reply.
- **Every incident becomes a test the same day** — and confirm it fails before
  you fix anything, because a regression test that passes on day one has not
  yet shown it can catch the failure. That requires persisted trajectories with correlation ids, designed
  in before the first incident.
